blogs.title: The Speculative Chain: D.C. Circuit Tightens Causation Standards in Enforcement Suits
blogs.description: This post analyzes the court's rigorous application of Article III causation and redressability doctrines. It focuses on Judge Katsas's rejection of the plaintiff's theory that an OSC investigation would inevitably lead to record production, highlighting the opinion's reliance on recent Supreme Court precedent (such as FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine) to sever the link between regulatory enforcement actions and ultimate relief for third parties. The analysis will explore how this ruling raises the bar for public interest groups seeking to compel agency investigations as a proxy for obtaining underlying substantive benefits.

blogs.title: Procedural Rights in Vacuo: Why Statutory Mandates Alone Cannot Confer Standing
blogs.description: Focusing on the distinction between procedural and substantive injuries, this article examines the court's refusal to grant standing based solely on the denial of a statutory right to an investigation. The post will dissect the application of Summers v. Earth Island Institute, explaining why the 'relaxed' standing standards for procedural violations still require a nexus to a concrete, particularized interest. It will discuss the implications for litigants who attempt to bypass traditional injury-in-fact requirements by pointing to congressional commands that agencies 'shall' act, even when the plaintiff has no guaranteed entitlement to the fruits of that action.

blogs.title: Statutory Silos: The Limits of Cross-Referencing Notice Provisions in FOIA Enforcement
blogs.description: This post explores the doctrinal tension between 5 U.S.C. § 1216 (OSC's general investigatory power) and § 1214 (procedures for prohibited personnel practices). It analyzes the court's rejection of the argument that triggering a § 1216 investigation automatically entitles a complainant to the notice and information protocols found in § 1214. The discussion will highlight how the D.C. Circuit navigated statutory interpretation to conclude that without an explicit statutory entitlement to specific information, a plaintiff cannot manufacture an 'informational injury' sufficient for Article III standing, effectively limiting the tools available to force transparency within internal agency watchdog processes.
